checks.prompt: A studio wants two things from a synthesis model: an animated character whose lines include laughter, hesitation and the occasional snatch of song, produced offline in batches; and a customer-service voice that must answer within a fraction of a second and say exactly the same words the same way every time. Which does this model suit, and why is the other a poor fit?
checks.explanation: This model is a next-token predictor over discrete audio codes rather than a phoneme-driven acoustic model, which is exactly why laughter, hesitation and singing are available to it — they are regions of the same token space it learned from raw audio. The cost is the other side of the same design: autoregressive generation is slow, one call produces only a short clip, and sampling makes it non-deterministic. Those three together rule it out for a low-latency, repeatable service voice.
options: The character. Because it learned from raw audio rather than a phoneme table, non-speech sounds are simply another region it can generate, and inline cues plus song markers make them reachable. The service voice is a poor fit on three counts: generation is slow and autoregressive, a single call is capped at roughly a dozen seconds, and it is stochastic by design, so identical text produces different audio each time
The service voice. Its strength is low-latency streaming with deterministic output, while expressive non-speech sounds require a specialised effects model
Both. Setting the sampling temperature to zero makes it deterministic and fast enough for interactive use, so the only difference is the wording of the prompt
Neither. It generates only music and sound effects; speech synthesis requires a conventional acoustic model and vocoder

checks.prompt: Explain this model as a language model for audio. Describe the three stages and what each contributes, name the trick that makes generating audio the same problem as generating text, and explain what a voice preset actually is. Then explain, in terms of that mechanism, why an inline cue for laughter can work at all — and why it is a hint rather than an instruction.
checks.expected: A correct answer must lay out the cascade: a first transformer maps text to semantic tokens capturing what to say and its prosody; a second produces the coarse codec tokens, the first few codebooks giving the gross structure of the sound; a third produces the remaining fine codec tokens carrying timbre and detail; and a neural codec decoder turns the full stack of tokens into a waveform. The enabling trick must be named: audio is quantised by a neural codec into sequences of small integers, so predicting the next audio token is the same kind of problem as predicting the next word — whereas predicting raw samples at tens of thousands per second is not tractable for such a model. A voice preset must be described as a saved tuple of tokens from the three stages that seeds generation, giving a consistent speaker, and the model's own output can be reused the same way for continuity between clips. The laughter question must be answered through the mechanism: because the model learned from raw audio rather than from a phoneme inventory, laughter is simply another region of token space it can visit, so a cue in the text can steer it there. Why it is only a hint follows from sampling: each stage samples from a distribution rather than executing a command, so the cue may be ignored, placed oddly, or produced somewhere else entirely — which is why generating several takes and choosing is the normal workflow. A strong answer notes that errors compound down the cascade, since each stage conditions on the previous one's output.

checks.prompt: A team tuning output quality asks what the two temperature settings do and why there are two of them. They also ask why pushing the value up gives them the laughter they wanted but sometimes garbles words. What is the right explanation?
checks.explanation: Temperature is the sharpness of the sampling distribution: turn it down and the most likely token nearly always wins, which is stable and lifeless; turn it up and the distribution flattens so rare tokens become reachable, which is where laughter and other characterful sounds come from. There are two settings because the stage that decides content is separate from the stages that produce sound, so you can keep the words stable while letting delivery vary. And the garbling is not a separate failure — making unlikely tokens likelier makes the wrong ones likelier too.
options: Temperature reshapes the sampling distribution: low values concentrate probability on the most likely token, producing flat and repetitive but safe output; high values flatten it so unlikely tokens — including the characterful, rare ones — actually get chosen. There are two because the content-deciding stage and the sound-producing stages are separate, so delivery can be loosened while content stays stable. The garbling is the same mechanism: raising the value makes ALL unlikely tokens likelier, including wrong words and artefacts
One temperature controls speed and the other controls quality; garbling means the model ran out of context and should be given shorter text
Temperature selects among the voice presets, so high values switch speaker mid-sentence, which is what sounds like garbling
Both temperatures control the codec's bit rate; raising them adds detail, and the garbling is quantisation noise that a finer codebook removes

checks.prompt: Implement the two ideas. First, residual quantisation. Write `make_codebook(values, k=8)` returning `k` entries interpolated at evenly spaced positions through the sorted values — so the first is the minimum and the last is the maximum — returning the median alone when `k` is 1 and raising `ValueError` for a `k` below 1 or an empty input. Write `quantize(values, codebook)` returning, for each value, the index of the nearest codebook entry. Write `rvq_encode(signal, codebooks)` returning one token stream per codebook, where each stage quantises the RESIDUAL left by the stages before it, and `rvq_decode(streams, codebooks)` returning the element-wise sum of the looked-up entries across all stages (an empty input gives an empty list). Write `rmse(a, b)` returning the root mean squared difference. Second, sampling. Write `softmax(logits, temperature=1.0)` returning the normalised exponentials of the logits divided by the temperature, computed stably, and raising `ValueError` for a temperature at or below zero. Write `entropy(probabilities)` returning the natural-logarithm entropy, skipping zero probabilities. Finally write `chunk_for_generation(sentences, max_seconds=13.0, seconds_per_char=0.06)` grouping consecutive sentences into chunks whose estimated durations sum to at most `max_seconds`, preserving order, raising `ValueError` — with a message mentioning the cap — if any single sentence exceeds it on its own. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The quantisation block is the enabling trick made small: a signal of floating-point values becomes streams of small integers, and stacking stages so that each encodes what the previous one missed is exactly the coarse-then-fine division of labour between the two sound-producing transformers. Note that the reconstruction improves with every stage and is never exact — the codec is lossy, and that is the trade being accepted in exchange for a sequence a next-token model can actually generate. The sampling block shows why the same knob gives both the personality and the failures: the favourite token never changes with temperature, but everything unlikely gets likelier together, so the setting that finally lets a laugh be emitted is the setting that also lets a wrong word be emitted. And the chunking function encodes the hard length cap — long narration is the caller's problem to split and stitch, and a single sentence that cannot fit is an error rather than something silently cut off.
checks.test:
import math

signal = [math.sin(2 * math.pi * 3 * i / 256) + 0.3 * math.sin(2 * math.pi * 11 * i / 256)
          for i in range(256)]

coarse_book = make_codebook(signal, 8)
assert len(coarse_book) == 8
assert coarse_book == sorted(coarse_book)
assert coarse_book[0] == min(signal) and coarse_book[-1] == max(signal)
assert len(make_codebook(signal, 1)) == 1
for bad in (lambda: make_codebook(signal, 0), lambda: make_codebook([], 4)):
    try:
        bad()
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError("must be refused")

# Encoding turns floats into small integers -- which is the entire reason a
# next-token model can generate audio at all.
tokens = quantize(signal, coarse_book)
assert len(tokens) == len(signal)
assert all(isinstance(token, int) and 0 <= token < 8 for token in tokens)
assert quantize([coarse_book[3]], coarse_book) == [3]

# Residual quantisation stacks: each stage encodes what the previous one missed,
# which is exactly the coarse-then-fine division of labour.
residual = [value - coarse_book[token] for value, token in zip(signal, tokens)]
fine_book = make_codebook(residual, 8)
streams = rvq_encode(signal, [coarse_book, fine_book])
assert len(streams) == 2 and streams[0] == tokens
assert all(0 <= token < 8 for token in streams[1])

coarse_only = rvq_decode(streams[:1], [coarse_book])
both = rvq_decode(streams, [coarse_book, fine_book])
assert len(both) == len(signal)
assert rmse(signal, both) < rmse(signal, coarse_only), (rmse(signal, both),
                                                        rmse(signal, coarse_only))
assert rmse(signal, both) > 0.0, "the codec is lossy, not exact"
assert rmse(signal, coarse_only) < rmse(signal, [0.0] * len(signal))

# Adding a third stage keeps improving it, with diminishing returns.
third_residual = [a - b for a, b in zip(signal, both)]
third_book = make_codebook(third_residual, 8)
three = rvq_decode(rvq_encode(signal, [coarse_book, fine_book, third_book]),
                   [coarse_book, fine_book, third_book])
assert rmse(signal, three) < rmse(signal, both)
assert rvq_decode([], []) == []

# Sampling: the temperature reshapes the same preferences without changing which
# one is preferred.
VOCAB = ["the", "cat", "[laughs]", "<pause>", "um", "♪"]
LOGITS = [3.0, 2.2, 0.8, 0.5, 0.3, -0.5]

cold = softmax(LOGITS, 0.3)
warm = softmax(LOGITS, 0.7)
hot = softmax(LOGITS, 1.5)
for distribution in (cold, warm, hot):
    assert abs(sum(distribution) - 1.0) < 1e-12
    assert all(p > 0 for p in distribution)
    assert distribution.index(max(distribution)) == 0, "the favourite never changes"

# Low temperature collapses onto the safe token -- flat, repetitive delivery.
assert cold[0] > 0.9, cold[0]
# High temperature is what actually lets the rare, characterful tokens be emitted.
assert hot[2] > warm[2] > cold[2], (cold[2], warm[2], hot[2])
assert hot[5] > 10 * cold[5], (cold[5], hot[5])
# ...and the same knob is what lets it go off the rails, because everything unlikely
# gets likelier at once.
assert entropy(hot) > entropy(warm) > entropy(cold)
assert entropy(cold) < 0.5 and entropy(hot) > 1.4, (entropy(cold), entropy(hot))
# A uniform distribution is the maximum-entropy case.
assert abs(entropy(softmax([0.0] * 6, 1.0)) - math.log(6)) < 1e-12
for bad in (0.0, -1.0):
    try:
        softmax(LOGITS, bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError("a non-positive temperature must be refused")

# A hard cap on the length of one generation means long narration is the caller's
# problem: split it, generate each piece, and stitch.
sentences = ["Hello there.", "This is a longer sentence for the model to say.",
             "And one more."]
chunks = chunk_for_generation(sentences, max_seconds=4.0)
assert [len(chunk) for chunk in chunks] == [2, 1], chunks
assert sum(len(chunk) for chunk in chunks) == len(sentences)
assert [s for chunk in chunks for s in chunk] == sentences, "order is preserved"
for chunk in chunks:
    assert sum(len(s) for s in chunk) * 0.06 <= 4.0
assert chunk_for_generation([]) == []
assert len(chunk_for_generation(["a"] * 100, max_seconds=1.0)) == 7
# A single sentence that cannot fit is an error rather than a silent truncation.
try:
    chunk_for_generation(["x" * 500])
except ValueError as exc:
    assert "cap" in str(exc), exc
else:
    raise AssertionError("an over-long sentence must be refused")

checks.prompt: A team automates narration and hits four problems: a test asserting the audio bytes match a stored fixture fails constantly; a paragraph comes back truncated; an inline cue for background music is ignored on most takes; and code copied from a tutorial does not match the interface they installed. What is the right assessment?
checks.explanation: Four separate realities of using this model. Sampling makes output different every call, so byte-comparison tests are simply the wrong test — seeding and pinning the preset reduces but does not remove drift. A single generation is capped at a short clip, so longer narration must be split, generated piecewise with the previous output seeding the next for continuity, and concatenated. Inline cues are suggestions to a sampler rather than commands, and effects cues are the least reliable of them. And there are two distinct interfaces to the same model whose calls differ, so mixing their documentation produces code that does not run.
options: Output is stochastic by design, so byte-equality is the wrong kind of test — seed the generator and pin the voice preset, and even then expect drift. The truncation is the per-generation length cap: split the text, generate each piece using the previous output as a seed for continuity, and concatenate. Cues are hints the sampler may ignore or misplace, and effects cues are the least reliable — generate several takes and choose. And there are two separate interfaces to this model whose function names and arguments differ, so snippets must match the one installed
The failing test means the model was loaded in training mode; the truncation is a token-limit setting to raise; cues require a separate effects model; and the interface mismatch is a version pin
All four are caused by insufficient memory, which silently truncates output, disables cues, changes the sampling seed and falls back to a legacy interface
The failing test indicates a corrupted download; the truncation means the text exceeded the vocabulary; cues only work in one language; and the two interfaces are aliases

checks.prompt: Position this model against a fast end-to-end neural synthesiser, a style-controllable model, a tiny on-device engine, a zero-shot cloning toolkit, and a hosted commercial service. Say when each wins. Then advise a game studio that needs hundreds of lines for a quirky non-player character — with laughs and mutters — plus in-game announcements generated on the fly on the player's machine. Say what you would use for each half and what practical workflow you would put around the first.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all five. This model wins on expressive, characterful audio with non-speech sounds and singing, multilingual out of the box, when offline batch generation is acceptable; it loses on speed, on the short per-generation cap, on determinism and on hardware appetite. The fast end-to-end synthesiser wins for high-quality, stable, repeatable speech in a fixed voice, without spontaneous expressiveness or built-in non-speech sounds. The style-controllable model wins on naturalness with explicit style and emotion control while remaining fast, at the cost of more setup and without the type-a-cue convenience. The tiny on-device engine wins on real-time synthesis with a minimal footprint, at the cost of sounding robotic and having no emotional range. The zero-shot cloning toolkit wins when reproducing a particular voice from a short clip is the requirement, though its range as a sound-design tool is narrower. The hosted commercial service wins on best-in-class quality, cloning and low latency, at the cost of being paid, closed and off-premises. The advice must split the two halves: the character's hundreds of lines are pre-recorded content generated offline, which is this model's case exactly; the on-the-fly announcements on a player's machine must be fast, deterministic and local, which points at the tiny on-device engine or a fast end-to-end synthesiser. The workflow around the first half must be concrete: split lines to respect the short generation cap, seed the voice with a fixed preset and reuse previous output for continuity, generate several takes per line because cues are hints rather than commands, and audition and pick — with the licensing point noted that cloning a specific real person's voice is restricted and the shipped presets are the sanctioned path.
